title: Distribution of Dentists According to Size of Dental Practice and Affiliation with a Dental Support Organization (DSO), 2025
measures: Share of practicing dentists by practice size (number of locations) and DSO affiliation, by career stage, sex and specialty. 2025 national: 17.0% DSO-affiliated (27.1% of dentists up to 10 years out of school; 31.4% of those 0-5 years out); 32.6% in '1 location & 1 dentist' (solo); by specialty DSO affiliation GP 16.3%, orthodontics 24.4%, pediatric 16.6%, OMS 24.7%, prosthodontics 11.3%; solo share GP 33.8%, orthodontics 36.6%, pediatric 21.1%. State DSO affiliation: Texas 23.3%, Florida 24.9%, Georgia 26.1%, California 12.1%.
limitations: Unit is dentists, not practices or offices. Analysis covers 198,110 of 211,761 practicing dentists. HPI states its method slightly undercounts DSO and large-group affiliation. DSO defined functionally (outside entity manages some or all non-clinical functions). Solo category excludes DSO-affiliated solo practices. Figures read from the XLSX data report linked on the page.

title: The State of the U.S. Dental Economy: 3rd Quarter 2026 Update
measures: Quarterly panel of dentists in private practice (704 responses in Q3 2026). In Q3 2026, 38% reported being not busy enough and able to treat more patients (26% in Q2 2026); 8% too busy to treat all patients requesting care. Average new-patient wait for an initial appointment among owner dentists accepting new patients was about 12 days. Around one-third of dentists were recruiting hygienists or assistants; most recruiting hygienists found it very or extremely challenging; about one in five reported hygienist positions open more than six months before being filled.
limitations: Self-reported panel of private-practice dentists; not a probability sample of practices. Quarterly figures move; read as conditions on the retrieval date. Figures read from the Q3 2026 PDF linked on the page.

title: Dental Care in Medicaid Programs (data report, December 2025)
measures: 41% of U.S. dentists participated in Medicaid/CHIP as of 2024, stable over a decade. Pediatric dentists have by far the highest participation of all dental specialists. 49% of DSO-affiliated dentists participated in 2024 (down from 67% in 2015) versus about two in five unaffiliated dentists. Medicaid fee-for-service reimbursement in most states falls far below 50% of dentist charges and 60% of private insurance reimbursement. Child Medicaid/CHIP beneficiaries have lower utilization than privately insured children and the gap is not shrinking.
limitations: Participation is defined as enrolment in the Insure Kids Now database or FQHC practice; it does not account for patient volume. State variation is large.

title: Coverage, Access & Outcomes: FAQs about dental coverage, access and outcomes
measures: Children ages 0-18: 56% have private dental benefits, 37% Medicaid or CHIP dental benefits, 7% no dental benefits. In 2024, 64% of children with private dental insurance had at least one dental visit, compared with 42% with public insurance and 26% with no dental insurance.
limitations: National figures from HPI's national trends report; not applicable to any one city or practice. Coverage shares and visit rates come from survey-based estimates.

title: Dental Care
measures: States are required to provide dental benefits to children covered by Medicaid and CHIP (Medicaid children through the EPSDT benefit); states choose whether to provide adult dental benefits and there are no minimum requirements for adult coverage. Separate CHIP programs may use a CHIP-compliant package or a benchmark dental package. States must post participating Medicaid and CHIP dental providers on InsureKidsNow.gov.
limitations: Federal framework only; benefits, fee schedules, managed-care arrangements and enrolment rules vary by state.

title: Recognized dental specialties
publisher: National Commission on Recognition of Dental Specialties and Certifying Boards
measures: Lists the 12 dental specialties currently recognized by the National Commission, including orthodontics and dentofacial orthopedics, pediatric dentistry, periodontics and prosthodontics. Cosmetic dentistry is not among them.
limitations: Recognition list can change; state dental boards set their own rules on specialty announcements.

title: ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct (2026 edition)
measures: Section 5.F: no dentist shall advertise in a manner that is false or misleading in any material respect; 5.F.2 examples include statements likely to create an unjustified expectation about results. 5.F.6: websites and SEO must be truthful. 4.E.1: paying a marketing vendor a percentage of professional fees collected from patients is fee splitting. 5.H: specialist announcements are limited to recognized specialties and dentists who meet the educational requirements.
limitations: Binds ADA members as professional ethics, not law; state dental board rules and state law may be stricter and govern. Read from the 2026 complete PDF linked on the page.
